revise.summary: I revised content/lessons/13-diagnosing-bugs.md. Both gates pass (no lint ERRORs; 14 tests ran and passed). The chat Scene now matches the 1.3.1 Skill: the agent shows its ranked hypotheses and keeps going without waiting (SKILL.md:98). Its hypotheses use the Skill's full prediction rule, "vanish or get worse" (SKILL.md:94), and the Scene is no longer set on this site, whose name field's maxLength would block 26 emoji. The Try it exercise now asks for the pause after the hypotheses, falls back to bash if neither Node nor Python is installed, and says where permission prompts, Esc and the plan-mode exit come in. The Bonus now says only what the repo holds (issue 03 line 12 and the PR #2 body). The human-in-the-loop advice now follows the template: the agent runs the script while you answer (template:4). In the Final test, scenario-flaky is replaced by spot-vague-symptom so goal 3 gets tested, and four other questions were reworked. I also fixed most reader terms (Phase, plan mode, Esc, /triage, TDD, push, issue, repo, ticket) and the Site story wording, which now claims only what the repo shows. The prose is 2,932 words: under the 3,000 limit but above the 2,800 target, because the glosses the reader findings asked for cost about 110 words even after cutting every section.

quiz.where: Steering it, and when to reach for it > checkpoint pause-first, prompt "before the agent changes any code" (line 182), option c "Turn on plan mode..." and its feedback (lines 187-188)
quiz.problem: The prompt asks for agreement "before the agent changes any code". The key (b) can't give that. Under the Lesson's own Phase 4, the agent adds tagged debug log lines to the code before it knows the root cause. Option c (plan mode) is the only option that holds back every edit until you approve, so a sharp reader can defend c. c's feedback is also false: it says plan mode means "the diagnosis can't start", but the docs say plan mode still runs shell commands to explore, so a curl or existing-test loop can go red. The same wording appears in the Scene (line 133), the steering bullet (line 167) and spot-vague-symptom (line 401), where option a's feedback says the request can be honoured.
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 110: "Every debug log gets a unique tag like `[DEBUG-a4f2]`, so one search finds them all at cleanup." Line 141: the Scene agent prints "`[DEBUG-7c1e] length=52 characters=26`" before "Shall I fix it?", though line 133 asked "Show me the root cause before you change any code." diagnosing-bugs/SKILL.md:110 "Tag every debug log with a unique prefix". https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes says plan mode means "Claude reads files, runs shell commands to explore, and writes a plan, but does not edit your source." Option c feedback: "Plan mode blocks edits, including the repro script and failing test the loop needs, so the diagnosis can't start."
quiz.fix:
Rewrite the Checkpoint (key stays b; lengths 59/51/53/65):
```checkpoint pause-first
You want to agree with the root cause before the agent starts fixing it. How do you get that pause?
- [ ] Nothing to do: it always waits for approval before the fix.
  > It doesn't. Only the hypothesis list is shown to you, and even that doesn't block.
- [x] Ask when you start: "show me the root cause first".
  > Right. The Skill has no pause before the fix, so say you want one when you invoke it.
- [ ] Choose No at its first permission prompt for an edit.
  > New sessions start in auto mode, so there may be no prompt at all, and its first edit is the repro or a debug log, not the fix.
- [ ] Watch closely and press Esc, which stops it, when the fix starts.
  > By then it's already changing code, and you never got to agree with the cause.
```
Also change "Show me the root cause before you change any code." to "Show me the root cause before you fix anything." at lines 133 and 401, and "show me the root cause before changing code" to "show me the root cause before you fix it" at line 167.

quiz.where: Final test spot-theory-first, prompt (line 377) and option c "Its only error is skipping the 3–5 ranked hypotheses." (lines 382-383)
quiz.problem: The scenario holds more than one real mistake. The agent theorises before it has a loop. It also offers a single guess with no prediction instead of 3–5 ranked ones, and it jumps to logs before showing a list. Option c names one of those real mistakes, and only the word "only" keeps it from being right. That is a wording trick, and a spot- question should contain one mistake to spot.
quiz.evidence: Prompt: "I think it's a timezone bug in the date helper. I'll add some logs to confirm." Lesson line 109: "Three to five ranked guesses at the cause, before testing any; a single guess tends to lock onto the first plausible idea." diagnosing-bugs/SKILL.md:90 "Generate **3–5 ranked hypotheses** before testing any of them."
quiz.fix:
Rewrite so the only mistake is the missing loop (key stays a; lengths 54/51/48/58):
```test spot-theory-first
A report says "the dashboard total is wrong after midnight". The agent opens four files, then shows four ranked hypotheses, each with a prediction. It hasn't run anything yet. Spot the mistake.
- [x] It's theorising before it has a command that goes red.
  > Right. Reading code to build theories before the loop exists is the exact failure the Skill blocks. First, a command that shows the wrong total.
- [ ] It should have read more files before ranking them.
  > More reading is still guessing. What's missing is a command that shows the wrong total.
- [ ] It should test them before showing you the list.
  > The list comes to you before testing. The real problem comes earlier: nothing has gone red yet.
- [ ] Timezone bugs can't be caught with a feedback loop at all.
  > They can: pin the clock to just after midnight and check the total. Pinning time is one way to make a loop deterministic.
```

quiz.where: Final test scenario-quick-question, prompt "What do you reply?" (line 329) and options b, c, d (lines 332-337)
quiz.problem: There is a wording tell. The prompt asks "What do you reply?", but only options a and d are replies in quotation marks. Options b (`/clear`) and c (plan mode) are actions, so the frame rules them out. That leaves a ("Carry on"), which contradicts the stated wish for a quick explanation. quiz.fix:
Rewrite with a neutral frame and parallel actions (key stays d; lengths 61/48/45/49):
```test scenario-quick-question
You ask: "Why might a row of buttons overflow on small screens?" You want a quick explanation, but the agent starts setting up a reproduction harness. What's your best move?
- [ ] Let it carry on; the loop will make the answer more accurate.
  > For a general question with no specific bug, a full diagnosis is slow overhead. The Skill is built for hard, specific defects.
- [ ] Type `/clear`, then ask the same question again.
  > The same words can trigger it again, because it's model-invoked. Say what you want instead.
- [ ] Turn on plan mode so it can't build anything.
  > That blocks edits but doesn't make it answer directly. Just tell it what you want.
- [x] Press Esc, then say you only want an explanation.
  > Right. It's model-invoked and sometimes fires on plain questions. Saying plainly what you want is the documented workaround.
```

If the prompts race past or it quits, open a second terminal window (on Windows, Git Bash from the Start menu, since PowerShell can't run bash scripts), type `bash` and a space followed by the script path the agent gives you, answer the prompts, and paste the `KEY=VALUE` lines back."

reader.where: Try it yourself, step 5: "Type `/clear` so the agent forgets what it planted." (line 242), with the step 4 prompt (line 239)
reader.problem: `/clear` empties the conversation but keeps Claude Code's project memory. Auto memory is on by default and is loaded into every new conversation. A note the planting agent saves ("this folder holds a planted bug in the total") would survive `/clear` and give the cause away, so the exercise can quietly fail.
reader.evidence: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands says "`/clear` starts fresh on a new task while keeping project memory." https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory says "Auto memory is on by default in local sessions", it is loaded into "Every session", and its `project` type holds "ongoing work ... that Claude can't derive from the code or git history".
reader.fix: Step 4 prompt: add "Don't save anything about this to memory." after "leave no hints in comments." Step 5: "Copy the command and both outputs somewhere, then type `/clear` so the agent forgets what it planted. (`/clear` keeps Claude Code's project memory, which is why step 4 asked it not to save anything.)"

reader.where: The six phases, gate by gate: "(its own word for its steps, not the Phase of [The context window](/learn/context-window))" (line 80)
reader.problem: For a reader arriving cold, the comparison names two things the Lesson never explains: Phase in Matt's sense and the context window. "The Phase of The context window" means nothing to them, so the clarification confuses more than it clears up.
reader.evidence: GLOSSARY.md:39-40 defines Phase as "A chunk of work inside one agent session, such as the grilling or the implementation". The Lesson never defines either term before line 80, and "context" first gets a clause at line 206.
reader.fix: "The Skill works in six phases, its own name for its steps. (Elsewhere in this course a Phase means a chunk of work inside one session; see [The context window](/learn/context-window).) Each phase sits behind a gate: the next can't start until something specific is true."

reader.where: Why it matters: "his README (the front page of his Skills' repository)" (line 24)
reader.problem: "Repository" is used with no explanation; the course's cold-reader list names repo as a term that needs a clause at first use. Its first explanation comes at line 263 ("Its repo (the project folder, tracked with Git)"). A Visitor who barely uses Git doesn't know what a repository is.
reader.evidence: Lesson line 24 vs line 263. writing-guide.md, "Lessons from the pilot review", says to define "... token, session, repo, spec, ticket ..." at first use, in a clause.
reader.fix: "... with a line his README (the front page of his Skills' repository, the online project folder that holds them) borrows from *The Pragmatic Programmer* ..." Line 263 can then shorten to "Its repo records a known quirk ...".

reader.where: The idea: "**Deterministic.** The same verdict on every run." (line 37) vs "Failing half the time is debuggable" (line 58)
reader.problem: The Lesson contradicts itself. A loop for a bug that comes and goes can never give the same verdict on every run, yet 21 lines later a loop that fails half the time is fine. The reader can't tell whether such a loop passes the Phase 1 gate. The Skill settles this with a flaky-bug clause that the Lesson leaves out.
reader.evidence: diagnosing-bugs/SKILL.md:62: "**Deterministic**: same verdict every run (flaky bugs: a pinned, high reproduction rate, per above)."
reader.fix: Line 37: "**Deterministic.** The same verdict on every run; for a bug that comes and goes, a steady, high failure rate (see below)."

reader.problem: Windows PowerShell 5.1 blocks scripts by default, so `npm install` often fails with "npm.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system". A Visitor who barely uses a terminal is stuck, and nothing in the Lesson or in Start here mentions it.
reader.evidence: This is a widely reported error, e.g. https://dev.to/jackfd120/resolving-npm-execution-policy-error-in-powershell-a-step-by-step-guide-for-developers-32ip ("npm : File C:\Program Files\nodejs\npm.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system"). `grep -n -i "execution policy\|npm.ps1" content/lessons/*.md` finds nothing.
reader.fix: After the sh block, add: "On Windows, if PowerShell says npm.ps1 cannot be loaded, type `npm.cmd install` instead."

reader.where: Final test, scenario-quick-question: "What do you reply?" (line 329)
reader.problem: The stem gives the answer away. It asks for a reply, but options b ("Type `/clear`, then ask the same question again.") and c ("Turn on plan mode so it can't build anything.") are actions, not replies. A test-savvy reader drops them on grammar alone and is left choosing between the two quoted replies.
reader.evidence: Lesson lines 330-337: options a and d are quoted replies; b and c are imperative actions.
reader.fix: Stem: "... but the agent starts setting up a reproduction harness. What's your best move?"

reader.where: Try it yourself, It's working if: "Debug logs carried a tag like `[DEBUG-xxxx]`, and none were left." (line 257)
reader.problem: In a tiny cart script the agent may test its predictions with a debugger or by changing inputs, and add no logs at all. A correct run then can't tick this box, and the reader may decide the Skill misbehaved.
reader.evidence: diagnosing-bugs/SKILL.md:106-107 puts "Debugger / REPL inspection if the env supports it" first and targeted logs second. The tag rule (:110) applies only to debug logs it actually adds.
reader.fix: "- [ ] If it added debug logs, each carried a tag like `[DEBUG-xxxx]`, and none were left."

reader.where: The six phases: the flow Scene captions (lines 91-104) and the numbered list (lines 107-112), including "If it made a test fail on purpose by editing code or test data, it compares against an untouched copy to prove the edit landed." (line 111)
reader.problem: The captions and the list say nearly the same things, and probes and regression tests are each defined twice (lines 99/110 and 101/111). The Lesson is at 2,932 prose words, above the 2,300-2,800 aim and close to the 3,000 lint cap. The forced-red sentence on line 111 is an edge case a first-time reader can't place (why would it make a test fail on purpose?).
reader.fix: Cut the line 111 sentence beginning "If it made a test fail on purpose". Drop the duplicate definitions from the list, e.g. line 110: "**Instrument.** Each probe tests one prediction, changing one thing at a time." and line 111: "**Fix and regression test.** It's written before the fix, but only at a correct seam ...".

reader.where: How Matt and others use it: "The AI Hero docs page suggests saying what you want" (line 213)
reader.problem: AI Hero is never introduced, so a cold reader doesn't know whose page this is or why it counts as the documented workaround that the scenario-quick-question feedback leans on.
reader.evidence: Lesson line 213. The only other mention is the sources entry at line 441.
reader.fix: "AI Hero, Matt's site of guides to his Skills, suggests saying what you want: "just answer this, don't diagnose"."

reader.where: Steering it, the table: "| A design question rather than a defect | `/prototype`; see [Prototype](/learn/prototype) |" (line 177)
reader.problem: It tells the reader to type `/prototype` without the course-wide caveat that a hidden Built-in also answers to that name, so the short name can fail.
reader.evidence: writing-guide.md, Facts: "A hidden Built-in also shadows `/prototype`; use `/mattpocock-skills:prototype` if the short name fails." content/lessons/04-grilling.md:166 and 12-main-flow.md:169 both add the caveat inline.
reader.fix: "| A design question rather than a defect | `/prototype` (or `/mattpocock-skills:prototype` if that says "unknown skill"); see [Prototype](/learn/prototype) |"

reader.where: Try it yourself, step 2: "If not, type `/exit`, install Matt's Skills, then run `claude` again:" (line 229)
reader.problem: The colon follows "run `claude` again", so the block underneath looks like the last step, but it is the install command that comes before it. A first-timer may run `claude` first, or wonder which line the block belongs to.
reader.evidence: Lesson lines 229-233. content/lessons/06-prototype.md:238 words the same step more clearly: "type `/exit`, run this, then run `claude` again:".
reader.fix: "If not, type `/exit`, run this install command, then run `claude` again:"
